name: Chin implant / genioplasty

lead: Chin augmentation adds or repositions chin projection so the chin balances the nose and jaw in profile. The two main routes are an implant placed over the bone and a sliding genioplasty, where a section of the lower jawbone is cut and moved forward, back, up or down.

An implant adds volume at the front of the chin; a sliding genioplasty moves bone together with the tissue attached to it. Reviews describe a bone-based correction as usually giving a more dramatic result, while implants are the simpler operation. Published work covers techniques, materials and stability, with little head-to-head research on which looks best.

paras: Implants go in through an incision inside the lip or under the chin; genioplasty is done from inside the mouth with plates and screws. People often pair it with a nose operation or jaw surgery. Forum users debate how many millimetres of advancement to aim for. Swelling settles over weeks and the result is judged after healing.

Reported problems include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip or chin numbness, infection, implant displacement or bone changes under implants, nerve injury and asymmetry. Neither approach corrects the bite. Both are done by plastic, facial plastic or oral and maxillofacial surgeons as regulated surgery.

angle.text: Chin implants and sliding genioplasty add or reposition chin projection to balance the profile, and the change is visible after healing. Both are routine surgeries, and forums describe bone sliding as the larger change.

lead: Chin augmentation, also called mentoplasty or genioplasty, changes the underlying structure of the chin to balance the rest of the face; it can add projection with an implant, reduce or round the chin through bone cutting, or change its height.[1] Sliding genioplasty uses an osteotomy of the chin bone, while implants are placed in a pocket over the bone, usually through an incision inside the mouth or under the chin.[1]

Reviews describe genioplasty as frequently done alone or with rhinoplasty, facelifts and orthognathic surgery and as an important element of lower-face aesthetics.[2][3] A bone-based correction is described as usually giving a more dramatic result than an implant, while implants are the simpler operation.[1][4] Neither approach corrects the bite.[1]
On looksmax.org, chin surgery is discussed as a way to improve the profile, with threads asking how much advancement to seek and whether genioplasty alone is enough.[5][6]
infobox: Alloplastic implant; sliding genioplasty (osteotomy); fillers or fat as non-surgical or adjunct options
Usually intraoral, or a skin incision under the chin
Rhinoplasty, jaw surgery, other facial procedures
Chin osteotomy techniques published in 1957 by Trauner and Obwegeser[8]

paras: Sliding genioplasty: a horseshoe-shaped piece of bone is cut from the lower edge of the mandible and moved forward to add projection or backward to reduce it, then fixed with a titanium plate and screws or with fine wires.[1] A technique developed by Korean surgeons, the T-osteotomy or mini V-line, narrows and lengthens the chin, with the mentalis muscle carefully reattached because it controls lower-lip and chin movement.[1]

Implants: materials include silicone, which is soft and can shift or cause bone resorption but is easy to remove; porous polyethylene (Medpor), which tissue grows into and which can be hard to remove; and ePTFE (Gore-Tex), which is flexible and often screwed to the bone.[1] A review of male facial implants notes that alloplastic implants provide the most predictable hard-tissue augmentation and discusses their most common and severe complications.[7]

Non-surgical options: temporary injectable fillers such as hyaluronic acid and calcium hydroxyapatite last months to years, while permanent fillers such as free silicone have fallen out of favour because of migration, inflammation and infection risks.[1]

Operating methods for chin reshaping and for correcting a small chin were described in two 1957 papers on mandibular surgery by Trauner and Obwegeser.[8][9] A 1989 review by a plastic surgeon described performing both osteotomies and implants in the late 1980s and called for greater use of genioplasty among aesthetic surgeons, while a 1988 review described implants as the most commonly used chin procedure and osteotomy as offering the greatest flexibility.[10][4]
Contemporary work includes resorbable fixation, piezoelectric bone cutting and computer-guided or patient-specific approaches.[11][12][13]

A 2024 review states that soft tissues around the mandible tend to return toward their original position despite secure osteotomy segments, an argument for careful planning.[2] A 2023 review of contemporary genioplasty covers its techniques, applications, stability, osteosynthesis and complications.[3] The Wikipedia article on chin augmentation says the procedure improves appearance but not dental occlusion.[1]

Controlled studies on genioplasty are mostly technical. A randomised trial compared two types of high labial incision, a randomised study examined piezosurgery, and a clinical study of 20 patients tested resorbable fixation, with most genial movements being advancements.[14][11][12] A 2024 randomised controlled trial evaluated soft-tissue profile changes after autogenous fat or onlay PEEK augmentation versus sliding genioplasty for a deficient chin.[13]

A study of 1,034 patients who underwent orthognathic surgery examined neurosensory function in the mental nerve region at two years after mandibular osteotomies including genioplasty.[15] Registered studies compare patient-specific alloplastic chin implants with computer-guided genioplasty and test the accuracy of patient-specific PEEK implants for chin deficiency.[16][17]

Common and usually minor effects of chin augmentation include swelling, hematoma and temporary lip weakness or numbness; less common are infection, bony changes under the implant, implant displacement and nerve damage.[1] Silicone implants may shift, buckle or erode bone, and donor bone grafts have been linked to a higher infection rate.[1]
A study of inferior alveolar nerve function after mandibular osteotomies reported measurable neurosensory deficits at two years after the sagittal split operation and also examined genioplasty.[15]

Threads ask whether a chin problem is better handled by genioplasty or by double-jaw surgery, and members share planning measurements, recovery experiences and removal stories.[5][6] One member reports that a surgeon proposed about 4 to 5 mm of advancement for an average chin and offered to extend the chin vertically to improve facial thirds.[6]

lore.intro: Chin surgery is one of the most frequently discussed procedures, with threads on genioplasty versus bimax, millimetre targets, recovery diets and complications.[5][6]

claims.claim: Sliding genioplasty gives a bigger, more reliable change than a chin implant.
A few millimetres of advancement is enough for an average chin.
A chin procedure alone may not solve a profile problem caused by the jaws.

timeline.event: Trauner and Obwegeser publish operating methods for chin reshaping and small chin correction.[8][9]
A review describes implants as the most commonly used chin procedure and osteotomy as the most flexible.[4]
A plastic surgeon's review argues for greater use of genioplasty in aesthetic practice.[10]
A study evaluates resorbable fixation in genioplasty.[11]
A randomised trial compares fat or PEEK onlay with sliding genioplasty.[13]
